Surprisals and surprisal probabilities of categorical data

Source: R/surprisals_factor.R
surprisals_factor.Rd

For a categorical variable taking one of the categories \(c_1,\dots,c_K\), the surprisal of an observation \(y\) is \(s = -\log f(y)\), where \(f(c_k)\) is the probability of category \(c_k\). The surprisal probability is the total probability of all categories that are no more probable than \(y\): $$p = \sum_{k=1}^K f(c_k) 1\big(f(c_k) \le f(y)\big).$$ Tied categories (with the same probability) have the same surprisal probability, which includes the probabilities of all of them.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'factor'
surprisals(object, prob = NULL, prior = 0, loo = FALSE, ...)

# S3 method for class 'factor'
surprisals_prob(
  object,
  approximation = c("none", "empirical", "rank"),
  threshold_probability = 0.1,
  prob = NULL,
  prior = 0,
  loo = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A factor.

prob

A numeric vector of probabilities for the levels of object, either named by level or in the order of levels(object). If NULL (the default), the probabilities are estimated from object.

prior

A non-negative constant \(a\) added to the count of each level when estimating the probabilities. Only used when prob is NULL.

loo

Should leave-one-out surprisals be computed? Only used when prob is NULL.

...

Other arguments are ignored.

approximation

Character string specifying the method to use in computing the surprisal probabilities. With "none" (the default), the exact probabilities are computed from the category probabilities. With "empirical" (or "rank"), the surprisal probability of each observation is the proportion of observations with greater or equal surprisals.

threshold_probability

Not used for categorical data.

Value

A numerical vector containing the surprisals or surprisal probabilities.

Details

By default, the probabilities are estimated from the data as \(\hat{f}(c_k) = (n_k + a)/(n + Ka)\), where \(n_k\) is the number of observations in category \(c_k\), \(n\) is the number of non-missing observations, \(K\) is the number of levels of object (including levels with no observations), and \(a\) is prior. This is the posterior mean of \(f(c_k)\) under a symmetric Dirichlet prior with parameter \(a\). With loo = TRUE, each observation is omitted when estimating the probabilities used for its own surprisal and surprisal probability, so that \(n_k\) and \(n\) are each reduced by one for an observation in category \(c_k\).

To compute surprisals of several categorical variables jointly, combine them into a single factor with interaction().

References

Hyndman, R J (2026) "That's weird: Anomaly detection using R", Chapter 7, https://OTexts.com/weird/density.html.

Hyndman, R J & Frazier, D T (2026) "Anomaly detection using surprisals", https://robjhyndman.com/publications/surprisals.html.

Author

Rob J Hyndman

Examples

# Road types of Australian road deaths since 2014
road_deaths |>
  filter(!is.na(road_type)) |>
  mutate(
    s = surprisals(road_type),
    p = surprisals_prob(road_type)
  ) |>
  count(road_type, s, p) |>
  arrange(p)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   road_type                     s        p     n
#>   <fct>                     <dbl>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1 Busway                     8.74 0.000160     2
#> 2 Pedestrian Thoroughfare    7.64 0.000638     6
#> 3 Access road                4.88 0.00822     95
#> 4 Collector Road             2.56 0.0854     968
#> 5 Sub-arterial Road          1.80 0.251     2077
#> 6 Local Road                 1.54 0.465     2677
#> 7 Arterial Road              1.45 0.698     2929
#> 8 National or State Highway  1.20 1         3782
# Joint surprisal probabilities of road user and sex
road_deaths |>
  filter(!is.na(road_user), !is.na(gender)) |>
  mutate(p = surprisals_prob(interaction(road_user, gender))) |>
  count(road_user, gender, p) |>
  arrange(p)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 4
#>    road_user                    gender       p     n
#>    <fct>                        <fct>    <dbl> <int>
#>  1 Motorcycle pillion passenger Male   0.00298   173
#>  2 Pedal cyclist                Female 0.00666   213
#>  3 Motorcycle pillion passenger Female 0.0104    218
#>  4 Motorcycle rider             Female 0.0153    286
#>  5 Pedal cyclist                Male   0.0392   1382
#>  6 Pedestrian                   Female 0.0891   2893
#>  7 Pedestrian                   Male   0.194    6064
#>  8 Passenger                    Female 0.300    6194
#>  9 Driver                       Female 0.412    6464
#> 10 Passenger                    Male   0.531    6906
#> 11 Motorcycle rider             Male   0.659    7428
#> 12 Driver                       Male   1       19761
